content.title: About
content.content: Beef kidneys are an organ meat from cattle, with a dense, slightly chewy texture and a strong, distinctive flavor. They are eaten in many cuisines, such as in steak and kidney pie in Britain, and in stews, sautés, and grills elsewhere. Kidneys are usually soaked and cleaned before cooking to reduce their strong smell.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kidneys act as the body's filter, so they have a strong, mineral flavor.
Steak and kidney pie is a classic British dish.
Soaking kidneys in water, milk, or vinegar water and removing the white core helps mellow the flavor.
Kidneys cook quickly but can become tough and strong-tasting if overcooked.
They are used in traditional dishes across Europe, Asia, and Latin America.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Rich in riboflavin
items.content: Riboflavin (B2) supports energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides selenium and iron
items.content: These minerals support antioxidant defenses, thyroid function, and oxygen transport.

items.title: Provides protein
items.content: Beef kidneys provide protein with relatively little fat.

items.title: Contains other B vitamins
items.content: Kidneys contain niacin and folate.

items.title: Purines
items.content: Kidneys are high in purines, which matters for people with gout or high uric acid.

items.title: Cholesterol
items.content: Kidneys are high in cholesterol, so people with certain health conditions should ask a healthcare professional about suitable amounts.

items.title: Contaminants
items.content: Kidneys can accumulate heavy metals such as cadmium, so eat them in moderation and choose reputable sources.

items.title: Kidney disease and foodborne illness
items.content: People with kidney disease should ask a healthcare professional about protein and phosphorus intake, and kidneys must be cooked thoroughly to at least about 71 °C (160 °F).

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beef kidneys should be trimmed of fat and the white core, soaked, and cooked thoroughly, for example sautéed in slices with onions, simmered in stews and pies, grilled on skewers, or braised. Do not overcook them or they become rubbery. Seasoning with acids such as lemon or vinegar balances their flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Beef kidneys are highly perishable. Keep them in the refrigerator and cook them within a day, or freeze them for longer storage. Cooked kidneys should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within three to four days. Discard any with a strong ammonia smell.

content.title: About
content.content: The chicken, rice & cheese burrito is a Mexican‑style dish consisting of a large soft wheat tortilla filled with seasoned grilled chicken, steamed rice, shredded cheese and often topped with salsa or sour cream. This combination provides a balanced mix of protein, carbohydrates and fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Burritos originated in northern Mexico where wheat flour tortillas were more common than corn.
Chicken is usually marinated in chili, cumin and lime for a distinctive flavor.
Mexican‑style rice is often cooked with tomato sauce and a hint of spices, giving it a richer taste.
Cheddar or Monterey Jack cheese melts smoothly, creating a creamy texture inside the burrito.
Because it is handheld, the burrito became a staple of fast‑food chains worldwide.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: Rice supplies complex carbohydrates that release energy slowly, helping you stay full longer.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Cheese adds calcium and phosphorus, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both chicken and rice contain B6 and B12 vitamins, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Adding vegetables such as lettuce or tomatoes boosts fiber content, beneficial for digestion.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Large burritos can be high in calories due to the tortilla, cheese and sauces, which should be considered in weight management.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheese and ready‑made sauces often contain salt; choose low‑sodium options if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or dairy protein allergy.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Chicken must be cooked to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F) to prevent salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The burrito is designed to be handheld; warm it in the microwave or on a skillet until the cheese melts. Serve with salsa, guacamole or sour cream to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared burrito in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For freezing, wrap tightly in plastic film and keep for up to 2 months; reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Burrito with beans and cheese is a Mexican dish consisting of a large soft wheat tortilla filled with cooked beans, melted cheese, and sometimes additional vegetables and spices. The tortilla is usually made from wheat flour, and the filling makes the dish hearty and protein‑rich.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The burrito originated in North Texas in the early 1920s and quickly spread throughout Mexico and the United States.
Beans used are often black or pinto, providing high fiber and slow‑release energy.
Cheese in traditional recipes is usually cheddar or Mexican “queso” that melts into a creamy texture.
Burritos are hand‑held, making them popular for on‑the‑go meals and picnics.
Variations may include rice, avocado, salsa, sour cream, and even grilled meat.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Beans and cheese together provide a substantial amount of protein needed for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Beans supply both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and blood‑sugar stability.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: Beans are a good source of iron and magnesium, which aid oxygen transport and nerve‑muscle function.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds calcium essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The burrito provides B1, B6, and folate, which are involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The tortilla, cheese, and beans make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese may cause discomfort for those who are lactose intolerant; lactose‑free alternatives can be used.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Cheese and ready‑made sauces often contain a lot of salt, which can be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Bean allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to beans and should choose different fillings.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Burritos are typically served hot. Heat them in a microwave or skillet, then fold tightly and eat with your hands. Add salsa, guacamole, or sour cream to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared burrito in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. It can be frozen for up to 2 months; reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

shrimp-and-vegetables-excluding-carrots-.title: Shrimp and vegetables without carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens; no potatoes, soy‑based sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp are a high‑protein seafood with low fat and rich in trace minerals such as iodine and selenium. The vegetables used in this dish can include bell pepper, zucchini, mushrooms, onion and tomato, providing a range of vitamins and minerals while excluding carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens, potatoes and soy‑based sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shrimp can change shell color depending on water temperature.
A 100 g serving of shrimp provides about 20 g of protein, making it an excellent protein source.
Vegetables like zucchini and bell pepper are high in vitamin C, which enhances iron absorption from seafood.
Shrimp contain astaxanthin, a powerful antioxidant that gives them their pink hue.
Steaming vegetables preserves most of their nutrients.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Shrimp deliver easily digestible protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: 100 g of shrimp contain roughly 85 kcal, making the dish suitable for weight management.

items.title: Source of iodine and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals support thyroid function and antioxidant defenses.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from vegetables
items.content: Bell pepper provides vitamins C and A, zucchini offers potassium and vitamin B6, mushrooms supply vitamin D and iron.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Low saturated fat and the presence of omega‑3 fatty acids in shrimp promote heart health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contain cholesterol, so people with hypercholesterolemia should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Pesticide residues on vegetables
items.content: Wash raw vegetables thoroughly to reduce pesticide residues.

items.title: Sodium in prepared sauces
items.content: Avoid soy‑based sauces, as they can add a high amount of salt.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté shrimp over medium heat for 2‑3 minutes until pink, then add sliced vegetables (bell pepper, zucchini, mushrooms, onion, tomato) and cook another 5‑7 minutes until tender. Finish with a splash of lemon juice and fresh herbs if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh shrimp refrigerated and use within 2 days; store the cooked dish in an airtight container for up to 3 days. Keep vegetables in a separate bag in the fridge to prevent excess moisture.
